entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 2
 
Ex 2:1-10. Birth and Preservation of Moses.

1. there went a man of the house of Levi, &c. Amram was the husband and Jochebed the wife (compare Ex 6:2; Nu 26:59). The marriage took place, and two children, Miriam and Aaron, were born some years before the infanticidal edict.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv595"/><div sID="gen847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv595"/><hi type="bold">6-9. when she had opened it, she saw the child--</hi>The narrative is picturesque. No tale of romance ever described a plot more skilfully laid or more full of interest in the development. The expedient of the ark, the slime and pitch, the choice of the time and place, the appeal to the sensibilities of the female breast, the stationing of the sister as a watch of the proceedings, her timely suggestion of a nurse, and the engagement of the mother herself--all bespeak a more than ordinary measure of ingenuity as well as intense solicitude on the part of the parents. But the origin of the scheme was most probably owing to a divine suggestion, as its success was due to an overruling Providence, who not only preserved the child's life, but provided for his being trained in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. Hence it is said to have been done by faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.23">He 11:23</reference>), either in the general promise of deliverance, or some special revelation made to Amram and Jochebed--and in this view, the pious couple gave a beautiful example of a firm reliance on the word of God, united with an active use of the most suitable means. <div eID="gen847" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv597"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.2.11-Exod.2.25">Ex 2:11-25</reference>. His Sympathy with the Hebrews.</title> <div sID="gen851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv597"/><hi type="bold">11. in those days, when Moses was grown--</hi>not in age and stature only, but in power as well as in renown for accomplishments and military prowess (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.22">Ac 7:22</reference>). There is a gap here in the sacred history which, however, is supplied by the inspired commentary of Paul, who has fully detailed the reasons as well as extent of the change that took place in his worldly condition; and whether, as some say, his royal mother had proposed to make him coregent and successor to the crown, or some other circumstances, led to a declaration of his mind, he determined to renounce the palace and identify himself with the suffering people of God (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.24-Heb.11.29">He 11:24-29</reference>). The descent of some great sovereigns, like Diocletian and Charles V, from a throne into private life, is nothing to the sacrifice which Moses made through the power of faith.<div eID="gen851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he went out unto his brethren--</hi>to make a full and systematic inspection of their condition in the various parts of the country where they were dispersed (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.23">Ac 7:23</reference>), and he adopted this proceeding in pursuance of the patriotic purpose that the faith, which is of the operation of God, was even then forming in his heart.<div eID="gen852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew--</hi>one of the taskmasters scourging a Hebrew slave without any just cause (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.24">Ac 7:24</reference>), and in so cruel a manner, that he seems to have died under the barbarous treatment--for the conditions of the sacred story imply such a fatal issue. The sight was new and strange to him, and though pre-eminent for meekness (<reference osisRef="Num.12.3">Nu 12:3</reference>), he was fired with indignation. <div eID="gen853" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv598"/><div sID="gen854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv598"/><hi type="bold">12. he slew the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand--</hi>This act of Moses may seem and indeed by some has been condemned as rash and unjustifiable--in plain terms, a deed of assassination. But we must not judge of his action in such a country and age by the standard of law and the notions of right which prevail in our Christian land; and, besides, not only is it not spoken of as a crime in Scripture or as distressing the perpetrator with remorse, but according to existing customs among nomadic tribes, he was bound to avenge the blood of a brother. The person he slew, however, being a government officer, he had rendered himself amenable to the laws of Egypt, and therefore he endeavored to screen himself from the consequences by concealment of the corpse. <div eID="gen854" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv599"/><div sID="gen855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv599"/><hi type="bold">13-14. two men of the Hebrews strove together--</hi>His benevolent mediation in this strife, though made in the kindest and mildest manner, was resented, and the taunt of the aggressor showing that Moses' conduct on the preceding day had become generally known, he determined to consult his safety by immediate flight (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">He 11:27</reference>). These two incidents prove that neither were the Israelites yet ready to go out of Egypt, nor Moses prepared to be their leader (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.20">Jas 1:20</reference>). It was by the staff and not the sword--by the meekness, and not the wrath of Moses that God was to accomplish that great work of deliverance. Both he and the people of Israel were for forty years more to be cast into the furnace of affliction, yet it was therein that He had chosen them (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Is 48:10</reference>). <div eID="gen855" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv601"/><div sID="gen859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv601"/><hi type="bold">16-22. the priest of Midian--</hi>or, "prince of Midian." As the officers were usually conjoined, he was the ruler also of the people called Cushites or Ethiopians, and like many other chiefs of pastoral people in that early age, he still retained the faith and worship of the true God.<div eID="gen859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven daughters--</hi>were shepherdesses to whom Moses was favorably introduced by an act of courtesy and courage in protecting them from the rude shepherds of some neighboring tribe at a well. He afterwards formed a close and permanent alliance with this family by marrying one of the daughters, Zipporah, "a little bird," called a Cushite or Ethiopian (<reference osisRef="Num.12.1">Nu 12:1</reference>), and whom Moses doubtless obtained in the manner of Jacob by service [see Ex 3:1]. He had by her two sons, whose names were, according to common practice, commemorative of incidents in the family history [Ex 18:3, 4]. <div eID="gen860" type="x-p"/>
